missing_spec_content.spec_text: The nucleus undergoing fission splits into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, and emits two or three neutrons plus gamma rays.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says the nucleus 'splits into two smaller nuclei' (keyPoints[0].content). It never says the two nuclei are roughly equal in size.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: All of the fission products have kinetic energy.
missing_spec_content.why: keyPoints[0].content says only 'The energy comes out as kinetic energy of the fragments and as gamma radiation.' It does not say that the emitted neutrons also have kinetic energy, which the spec requires when it says all fission products do.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Spontaneous fission is rare. Usually, for fission to occur the unstable nucleus must first absorb a neutron.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never mentions spontaneous fission. It presents neutron absorption as the only way fission happens.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to draw/interpret diagrams representing nuclear fission and how a chain reaction may occur.
missing_spec_content.why: Every keyPoint has "diagram": null. The lesson gives no fission or chain-reaction diagram for the student to interpret. Only keyPoints[1].tutor_note says 'Be able to draw or describe the chain reaction diagram'.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: In this process some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson links fusion energy to a mass change: 'Both processes release energy because of a small change in nuclear mass' (keyPoints[3].content). It never states the spec point that the mass is converted into the energy of radiation.

above_gcse.text: Each fission reaction releases about 200 MeV. A chemical reaction releases only a few eV. That is about 50 million times less.
above_gcse.why: The MeV/eV energy units and these numerical values are not required by the spec sections.

above_gcse.text: ~17.6 MeV per D-T reaction, but more per kg of fuel
above_gcse.why: A quantitative energy per reaction for fusion is not required, and it may confuse the student when set beside the 200 MeV figure for fission.
The spec requires only the general definition of fusion ('joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus'). It does not require the specific deuterium–tritium reaction equation.

above_gcse.text: Control rods: these absorb extra neutrons... They are made of boron or cadmium. - Moderator: this slows neutrons down to the right speed for U-235 to absorb them. It is usually water or graphite.
above_gcse.why: The spec says only that 'The chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor'. Reactor components, their materials and neutron moderation are not in these spec sections.

above_gcse.text: Challenge: it needs extremely high temperatures (~100 million °C on Earth) and pressures. These overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei.
above_gcse.why: The conditions needed for fusion, electrostatic repulsion and specific temperatures are not in spec section 4.4.4.2.

above_gcse.text: This mass difference is converted to energy by E = mc².
above_gcse.why: E = mc² is not part of the spec sections given. The intro also builds on it: 'When Einstein wrote E = mc²...'

above_gcse.text: Fission advantages: proven technology and large-scale electricity generation... Fusion disadvantages: ... People joke that it is 'always 30 years away'.
above_gcse.why: Evaluating nuclear power as an energy resource is not in spec sections 4.4.4.1–4.4.4.2. Checkpoint 3 tests this content.

above_gcse.text: A fissile isotope used as fuel in nuclear reactors; splits when it absorbs a slow neutron
above_gcse.why: The term 'fissile' and the slow-neutron condition are not required by the spec.

factual_errors.text: A large nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing 2–3 neutrons and a large amount of energy
factual_errors.correction: Fission is defined as the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus. Neutron absorption is the usual trigger but not the only one: spontaneous fission occurs, though it is rare.
Deuterium can be extracted from seawater. Tritium, the other fuel in the D-T reaction the lesson describes, is very scarce in nature. It must be produced (bred) from lithium.

factual_errors.text: Fusion uses hydrogen isotopes as fuel, not uranium. They are plentiful.
factual_errors.correction: Deuterium is plentiful. Tritium is not plentiful naturally and must be bred from lithium.

factual_errors.text: Fusion's main product is helium. Its radioactivity is much shorter-lived than that of fission fragments.
factual_errors.correction: Helium-4 is not radioactive. The radioactivity linked to D-T fusion comes from the tritium fuel and from reactor materials made radioactive by fusion neutrons, not from the helium product.

wrong_terms.text: two small nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus
wrong_terms.spec_term: two light nuclei ... a heavier nucleus

wrong_terms.text: splits into two smaller nuclei, called fission fragments

not_checked: No diagrams are present (every keyPoint has "diagram": null), so there was no diagram content to check against the spec's drawing/interpreting requirement.
The checkpoint keys "0"–"3" were assumed to correspond to keyPoints[0]–[3].
The statistic 'about 10% of the world's electricity' (intro) and the core temperature '~15 million °C' (keyPoints[2].content) were checked only approximately, from general knowledge.
